13: # sk-code Handoff Schema
14: 
15: Envelope for when an extracted Style Reference DESIGN.md moves to `sk-code` implementation. This file defines the contract shape; the extraction fills the subset it owns and keeps extraction judgment in this skill.
16: 
17: ---
18: 
19: ## 1. OVERVIEW
20: 
21: ### Purpose
22: 
23: Keep the design-to-build boundary explicit. This skill decides the measured design reference, its locked values, and its risks. `sk-code` implements the accepted handoff in the detected stack, verifies it, and raises conflicts when the target surface cannot honor the card.
24: 
25: ### Usage
26: 
27: Use this schema whenever an accepted Style Reference (measured tokens, components, and provenance) is handed to `sk-code`. Add required fields as needed, but do not rename the shared envelope fields.
28: 
29: ---
30: 
31: ## 2. COMMON ENVELOPE
32: 
33: Every handoff card uses this order. Mark a field `N/A` only when the extraction truly does not own it.
34: 
35: | Field | Required Content |
36: |---|---|
37: | **WHAT** | The deliverable being handed off: the Style Reference DESIGN.md plus its token data. Include the source surface and current state. |
38: | **LOCKED VALUES** | Exact measured values `sk-code` must use verbatim: colors, type roles, spacing, breakpoints, durations, easing, copy strings, or other pinned values. |
39: | **SIGNATURE MOVES** | Distinctive elements the reference captured. Name the visual, structural, or temporal moves that make the source specific. |
40: | **REUSE LIST** | Existing components, tokens, patterns, routes, or systems to reuse. State what must not be rebuilt. |
41: | **IMPLEMENTATION MECHANISM / STACK BOUNDARY** | The library, framework, or implementation mechanism that applies. State what `sk-code` owns and what the reference already decided. |
42: | **OPEN RISKS / VERIFICATION** | Risks `sk-code` must check, with severity and owner: accessibility, responsive, performance, fidelity, and residual uncertainty (including any inferred-vs-measured token). |
43: | **NEVER-CHANGE** | Constraints `sk-code` must not alter: URLs, nav labels, form fields, legal copy, locked tokens, or component contracts. |
44: 
45: ---
46: 
47: ## 3. EXTRACTION HANDOFF NOTE
48: 
49: A Style Reference handoff carries the provenance the extraction recorded. Every LOCKED VALUE traces to a source observation, and any value the reference labeled inferred (not measured) is flagged as an OPEN RISK so `sk-code` never treats an inferred token as ground truth.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 4. HANDOFF RULES
54: 
55: 1. **Design owns decisions.** `sk-code` implements the handed-off decision and raises conflicts instead of redesigning it silently.
56: 2. **Values stay exact.** Locked measured values are copied verbatim unless implementation proves they fail accessibility or platform constraints.
57: 3. **Reuse beats rebuild.** The reuse list is a constraint, not a suggestion.
58: 4. **Provenance travels.** Measured-vs-inferred labels survive the handoff; `sk-code` verifies inferred values before relying on them.
59: 5. **Stack boundaries are real.** The handoff names the mechanism so `sk-code` does not migrate or mix systems by accident.

17: # DESIGN.md Writing Style Guide
18: 
19: Writing quality standard for the v3 **Style Reference** output (see `design-md-format.md`). This guide governs the prose voice only — named and restrained, not mechanical and hedged.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: The Style Reference is a named, role-driven, ship-ready design-system handoff — not an extraction report. Every value still traces verbatim to `tokens.json`. Write like a design-systems lead handing the system off to the team that will ship it tomorrow. The reader already knows CSS, typography, and color theory -- never explain fundamentals.
26: 
27: **Division of labour (read this first).** In the v3 pipeline the value-bearing sections — `## Tokens — Colors`, `## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes`, `## Surfaces`, and `## Quick Start` — are pre-rendered deterministically by `backend/scripts/formatters-v3.ts` (a hue+lightness colour-namer and emitters) and pasted into the doc unchanged. The agent writes **prose only** (header, intro, Typography role prose, Components, Do's/Don'ts, Elevation, Imagery, Layout, Agent Prompt Guide, Similar Brands). You never hand-author a value table, so "100rem where the tokens say 100%" cannot happen — this guide is about making the prose worthy of the named tokens, not about transcribing numbers.
28: 
29: **Voice characteristics — named, confident, restrained:**
30: - **Named.** Colours, components, and surfaces carry evocative, grounded names (Obsidian Ink, Voltage, Primary CTA, Canvas), never "Color 1" or "Variant-1". Naming is a grounded inference about hue, lightness, and role — it is allowed and expected.
31: - **Confident.** State roles plainly and assign Similar Brands as grounded inference. Do not hedge every sentence with "appears to" or "seems". You are characterizing what IS there.
32: - **Restrained.** One grounded clause, not a paragraph of metaphor. "A warm-tinted near-black" beats "letters like hull plates." No purple prose.
33: - **Honest.** Confident never means inventing a SYSTEM the data contradicts. No "gradient-as-depth" with 0 shadow tokens, no "focus is consistent" when `focusIndicator.consistent` is false. Name and characterize what exists; never assert a relationship the tokens deny.
34: - **Dense, not noisy.** Every sentence carries one piece of implementation-changing information. But never dump raw mechanics: no frequency counts ("border 9685, text 4258"), no extractor-internal var names (`--_color-primitives---neutral--1400`), no DOM-tag labels ("div"). Frequency DECIDES prominence and role; it is never printed.
35: 
36: **Audience model:** A frontend engineer absorbing the system before building a component. Do NOT assume a market audience the page never states ("targets captains and port agents") — characterize the design, not an imagined user.
37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 2. BANNED WORDS
41: 
42: NEVER use these words in descriptive prose. They communicate nothing specific and signal that the writer ran out of things to observe:
43: 
44: `clean`, `modern`, `sleek`, `professional`, `user-friendly`, `intuitive`, `elegant`, `beautiful`, `stunning`, `gorgeous`, `polished`, `refined`, `sophisticated`, `seamless`, `cutting-edge`, `state-of-the-art`, `next-generation`, `innovative`, `revolutionary`, `world-class`, `premium` (when used as a vague adjective rather than a pricing tier), `crisp`, `delightful`, `lovely`, `nice`, `simple` (when used approvingly without specifics)
45: 
46: **The replacement rule:** Every banned word is a placeholder for a specific observation you have not yet made. Find the observation.
47: 
48: | Banned phrase | What to write instead |
49: |---|---|
50: | "clean design" | "gallery-like emptiness where section padding exceeds 80px and the only color signal comes from three workflow-specific accents" |
51: | "modern typography" | "Inter Variable at weight 510 with OpenType `cv01` and `ss03` -- a between-weight that creates emphasis without the heaviness of traditional medium" |
52: | "sleek interface" | "near-black canvas (`#08090a`) where content emerges through four luminance steps of semi-transparent white backgrounds" |
53: | "professional color palette" | "achromatic system with a single chromatic accent (`#5e6ad2`) reserved exclusively for interactive elements" |
54: | "intuitive layout" | "single-column hero with 80-120px vertical padding, collapsing to 2-3 column card grids at the feature section level" |
55: | "elegant shadows" | "multi-layer shadow stacks where blue-tinted `rgba(50,50,93,0.25)` sits at 30px offset while neutral `rgba(0,0,0,0.1)` sits closer at 18px, creating parallax depth" |
56: 
57: ---
58: 
59: ## 3. HEADER — TAGLINE RULES
60: 
61: The header is a title line, an evocative `> tagline`, and a `**Theme:**` line:
62: 
63: ```
64: # <Brand or Domain> — Style Reference
65: > <one-line evocative tagline — the design's essence in a phrase>
66: 
67: **Theme:** light | dark | mixed
68: ```
69: 
70: The **tagline** is a single grounded, evocative phrase. It must do three things simultaneously:
71: 
72: 1. **Capture the design system's essence** -- not its parameters, but its character and position
73: 2. **Use a precise framing** that makes this system distinguishable from every other
74: 3. **Let a reader who has never seen the site form a mental image** that would survive comparison with the real thing
75: 
76: ### What the tagline is NOT
77: 
78: - A parameter list: "Uses Inter font, dark backgrounds, and purple accents."
79: - A compliment or banned word: "A beautifully designed, modern system."
80: - A bare category label: "A minimalist dark-mode design system."
81: - An invented fact about the brand or its audience.
82: 
83: ### What the tagline IS
84: 
85: An essence capture -- one phrase that makes someone say "I know exactly what this looks like." It characterizes; it never fabricates a fact.
86: 
87: ### Example taglines
88: 
89: > Broadsheet financial broadside — the masthead itself is the design
90: 
91: > A near-black canvas where content emerges through four luminance steps
92: 
93: > Developer infrastructure made invisible — restraint as a thesis
94: 
95: ### Tagline test
96: 
97: Ask: "Could this phrase describe three other sites?" If yes, it fails. A tagline must be so specific that swapping it onto a different site would feel wrong.
98: 
99: ---
100: 
101: ## 4. INTRO PARAGRAPH
102: 
103: Directly under the header, one unlabeled paragraph of **4-6 sentences**. It characterizes the system's voice across these dimensions: the canvas, the dominant type move, how colour is rationed, layout density, and what carries the page. Every characterizing claim must map to a real token (a hex, a size, a weight). Restrained, not purple. No assumed audience unless the page states it.
104: 
105: > "The canvas is a warm-tinted near-black (`#121613`), with Obsidian Ink doing double duty as text, borders, and image frames. A single high-voltage accent (`#06458c`) is rationed strictly to interactive elements — everything else is neutral by default. Display type runs at 140px with -1.4px tracking against a 16px body, so hierarchy comes from scale, not weight. Section rhythm is spacious: large gaps frame each block as self-contained. The system is flat — no shadow tokens — and depth is carried by border contrast and whitespace alone."
106: 
107: Note: every claim cites a real value, colours are named (Obsidian Ink, the accent), the flat-elevation truth is stated plainly rather than dressed up as "gradient-as-depth", and there is no invented audience.
108: 
109: ### Intro test
110: 
111: Each sentence should be deletable without making the others incomprehensible, but their combined effect is a complete picture: canvas → type → colour rationing → layout → what carries depth. A sentence with zero values is an opinion — cut it or ground it.
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 5. KEY CHARACTERISTICS FORMAT
116: 
117: Each key characteristic follows a strict two-part structure joined by an em-dash:
118: 
119: ```
120: - [Design intent / what it achieves] -- [implementation parameters / how to do it]
121: ```
122: 
123: The front half tells you WHY. The back half tells you WHAT. Neither half works alone.
124: 
125: ### Good key characteristics
126: 
127: ```
128: - Geist Sans with extreme negative letter-spacing (-2.4px to -2.88px at display) -- text as compressed infrastructure
129: - Shadow-as-border technique: `box-shadow 0px 0px 0px 1px` replaces traditional borders throughout
130: - Weight 300 as the signature headline weight -- light, confident, anti-convention
131: - Dark-mode-native: `#08090a` marketing background, `#0f1011` panel background, `#191a1b` elevated surfaces
132: ```
133: 
134: ### Bad key characteristics
135: 
136: ```
137: - Uses a nice dark color palette (no values, no contrast, "nice" is banned)
138: - The font is Inter (no weight, no features, no personality)
139: - Has good spacing (no values, no philosophy)
140: - Borders are thin (how thin? what technique? why?)
141: ```
142: 
143: ### Quantity
144: 
145: 8-12 key characteristics. Fewer means you missed something. More means you are listing parameters instead of characteristics. A characteristic is a parameter + its design significance.
146: 
147: ---
148: 
149: ## 6. COLOUR NAMING (`## Tokens — Colors`)
150: 
151: In v3 the colour table is **pre-rendered** by `formatters-v3.ts` in the `Name | Value | Token | Role` shape, most-prominent first. You do not hand-author it — but you must understand the naming style, because the Quick Start re-uses these exact slugs and the rest of your prose references colours by their names.
152: 
153: ```
154: | Name | Value | Token | Role |
155: |------|-------|-------|------|
156: | Obsidian Ink | `#121613` | `--color-obsidian-ink` | Primary text, borders, image frames — a warm-tinted near-black |
157: | Voltage | `#06458c` | `--color-voltage` | Interactive elements only — do not promote it to a static text colour |
158: ```
159: 
160: Each column has a job:
161: 
162: 1. **Name** — evocative + grounded (hue + lightness + character). Neutrals by lightness (Snow/Linen → Ink/Obsidian/Void); hued by family + character (Voltage/Azure/Ember/Sage/Mist). Be consistent within a doc.
163: 2. **Value** — 6-digit lowercase hex, verbatim. Gradients render their full `linear-gradient(...)` value.
164: 3. **Token** — `--color-<kebab-name>` derived from the Name. NEVER the extractor's internal `--_color-primitives` var.
165: 4. **Role** — where it is used (grounded in measured usage) plus one characterizing clause. No frequency numbers. For a supporting accent, add a usage guard ("Do not promote it to the primary CTA color").
166: 
167: ### Good role clauses
168: 
169: > Primary text, borders, image frames — a warm-tinted near-black
170: 
171: > Card surfaces — same hex as canvas, so cards are defined by radius and padding, not fill
172: 
173: ### Bad role clauses
174: 
175: > Used for buttons. (No character, no usage guard)
176: 
177: > The colour that appears 9685 times. (Frequency dump — frequency decides prominence, it is never printed)
178: 
179: > `--_color-primitives---neutral--1400`. (Extractor-internal var leaked into the token column)
180: 
181: ### The characterizing clause
182: 
183: It describes visual quality, not emotional reaction, and never restates the hex in words. "A warm-tinted near-black" tells you something measurable. "Beautiful dark colour" does not. L1/L2 colours go in the main table; L3 in a `### Current Campaign Colors (Subject to change)` sub-table; L4 is excluded entirely.
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 7. VALUE EMBEDDING
188: 
189: Design values (font sizes, letter-spacing, weights, hex codes, opacity values) must be woven into prose. They never stand alone as facts.
190: 
191: ### The rule
192: 
193: A value without context is a spec sheet entry. A value inside a sentence that explains its effect is design documentation.
194: 
195: ### Good value embedding
196: 
197: > "The aggressive negative letter-spacing (-2.4px at display sizes) creates text that feels minified for production."
198: 
199: > "The 510 weight sits between regular and medium, creating a subtle emphasis that doesn't shout."
200: 
201: > "Individual shadow layer opacity never exceeds 0.05, producing ambient occlusion that feels like natural light rather than computer-generated depth."
202: 
203: ### Bad value embedding
204: 
205: > "Letter spacing: -2.4px. This creates compression."
206: 
207: Two sentences where one would do. The value and its effect are separated, making the reader do assembly work.
208: 
209: > "The letter-spacing is -2.4px."
210: 
211: A fact with no consequence. Why should someone care that it is -2.4px? What does -2.4px produce that -1px or -0.5px does not?
212: 
213: > "Font size: 48px, Weight: 600, Line height: 1.00, Letter spacing: -2.4px"
214: 
215: A parameter dump. This belongs in a table, not in prose. Prose exists to explain what tables cannot: the relationships between parameters and the reasons behind choices.
216: 
217: ### Where values DO stand alone
218: 
219: Tables, component specs, and agent prompt guides. These are reference contexts where scanability matters more than narrative. In those contexts, every value should be present and findable. In prose sections, values are evidence for claims.
220: 
221: ---
222: 
223: ## 8. DO'S AND DON'TS QUALITY
224: 
225: The Do's and Don'ts section is where most DESIGN.md files fail. Generic advice wastes the reader's time. Every entry must pass the specificity test.
226: 
227: ### Don'ts: The Counter-Intuitive Test
228: 
229: A good Don't tells the reader something they would naturally do that is WRONG in this specific system. It should surprise someone who knows CSS and design but does not know this particular system.
230: 
231: **Each Don't needs three components:**
232: 1. What not to do
233: 2. Why it is wrong in THIS system (not in general)
234: 3. What to do instead (with at least one specific value)
235: 
236: ### Good Don'ts
237: 
238: > "Don't use weight 600-700 for sohne-var headlines -- weight 300 is the brand voice"
239: 
240: Counter-intuitive: most systems use heavy weights for headlines. The reader would default to 600+ without this warning.
241: 
242: > "Don't skip the inner `#fafafa` ring in card shadows -- it's the glow that makes the elevation system work"
243: 
244: Counter-intuitive: a developer building a card shadow would include the obvious layers (border, elevation) and skip the inner ring because it seems decorative. This Don't explains that it is structural.
245: 
246: > "Don't use solid colored backgrounds for buttons -- transparency is the system (rgba white at 0.02-0.05)"
247: 
248: Counter-intuitive: every instinct says to give buttons a solid background color. Linear's system is built on near-zero opacity.
249: 
250: ### Bad Don'ts
251: 
252: > "Don't use too many colors"
253: 
254: No threshold, no alternative, applicable to every design system ever created.
255: 
256: > "Don't forget accessibility"
257: 
258: Not a design system rule. This is a general web development principle.
259: 
260: > "Don't make things too large"
261: 
262: Too large relative to what? No values, no system-specific context.
263: 
264: ### Do's: The Implementation Shortcut Test
265: 
266: A good Do gives a reader an implementation shortcut. After reading it, they should be able to write correct CSS faster.
267: 
268: ### Good Do's
269: 
270: > "Use shadow-as-border (`0px 0px 0px 1px rgba(0,0,0,0.08)`) instead of traditional CSS borders"
271: 
272: Gives the exact value and names the technique. A developer can copy this into their code immediately.
273: 
274: > "Use `#171717` instead of `#000000` for primary text -- the micro-warmth matters"
275: 
276: Names both the correct value AND the common mistake, with a one-phrase rationale.
277: 
278: ---
279: 
280: ## 9. AGENT PROMPT GUIDE
281: 
282: Agent prompts must be SELF-CONTAINED. A developer copies one prompt into an AI tool and gets a correct component without needing the rest of the DESIGN.md.
283: 
284: ### Requirements
285: 
286: - **Complete hex values** for every color mentioned
287: - **Font family, size, weight, and line-height** for every text element
288: - **Letter-spacing** where the system uses non-default tracking
289: - **Padding, radius, and shadow values** for every container or interactive element
290: - **OpenType features** if the system uses them
291: - **100-200 words each** -- long enough to be complete, short enough to fit in a prompt window
292: 
293: ### Good agent prompt
294: 
295: > "Create a hero section on white background. Headline at 48px Geist weight 600, line-height 1.00, letter-spacing -2.4px, color #171717. Subtitle at 20px Geist weight 400, line-height 1.80, color #4d4d4d. Dark CTA button (#171717, 6px radius, 8px 16px padding) and ghost button (white, shadow-border rgba(0,0,0,0.08) 0px 0px 0px 1px, 6px radius)."
296: 
297: Every value is present. No lookups required.
298: 
299: ### Bad agent prompt
300: 
301: > "Create a hero section using the brand colors and primary font. Make the headline large and the subtitle smaller. Add a primary and secondary button."
302: 
303: Every value is missing. The AI tool would guess, and every guess would be wrong.
304: 
305: ### Prompt coverage
306: 
307: Include prompts for at least:
308: - Hero section
309: - Card component
310: - Badge/pill
311: - Navigation
312: - One system-specific component (workflow pipeline, command palette, dark section)
313: 
314: ---
315: 
316: ## 10. INFORMATION DENSITY
317: 
318: ### The deletion test
319: 
320: Read every sentence. Ask: "If I delete this, does the reader lose implementation-relevant information?" If no, delete it.
321: 
322: ### Banned transition phrases
323: 
324: Never write:
325: - "Let's look at..."
326: - "In this section, we'll explore..."
327: - "Now let's move on to..."
328: - "As we can see..."
329: - "It's worth noting that..."
330: - "It's important to mention..."
331: - "Another key aspect is..."
332: 
333: These phrases exist in drafts. They do not exist in published technical writing. They add words without adding information.
334: 
335: ### No restating tables
336: 
337: If a value appears in a table, do not repeat it in the prose below the table unless the prose adds NEW information about that value (rationale, relationship to another value, historical context).
338: 
339: ### Paragraph density target
340: 
341: Each prose paragraph (intro, Typography role prose, Layout, Elevation) should contain 2-4 concrete values (hex codes, pixel values, weights, opacities). A paragraph with zero values is an opinion. A paragraph with one value is an observation. A paragraph with 2-4 values is documentation.
342: 
343: ---
344: 
345: ## 11. TEN GOOD/BAD WRITING COMPARISONS
346: 
347: ### 1. Atmosphere Description
348: 
349: **BAD:**
350: > "The website has a clean, modern design with a dark color scheme that looks very professional and sleek."
351: 
352: **GOOD:**
353: > "Linear's website is a masterclass in dark-mode-first product design -- a near-black canvas (`#08090a`) where content emerges from darkness like starlight. The overall impression is one of extreme precision engineering: every element exists in a carefully calibrated hierarchy of luminance, from barely-visible borders (`rgba(255,255,255,0.05)`) to soft, luminous text (`#f7f8f8`)."
354: 
355: **Why the good version works:** Three specific values, a metaphor that communicates visual quality ("starlight"), and a structural observation (luminance hierarchy) instead of a vague adjective.
356: 
357: ---
358: 
359: ### 2. Color Description
360: 
361: **BAD:**
362: > "The primary color is a nice shade of purple (#533afd) that is used for buttons and links."
363: 
364: **GOOD:**
365: > "**Stripe Purple** (`#533afd`): Primary brand color, CTA backgrounds, link text, interactive highlights. A saturated blue-violet that anchors the entire system. This isn't the cold, clinical purple of enterprise software; it's a rich, saturated violet that reads as confident."
366: 
367: **Why the good version works:** Names the color, lists all its roles (not just buttons), provides a personality sentence, and contrasts it with what it is NOT (cold, clinical enterprise purple).
368: 
369: ---
370: 
371: ### 3. Key Characteristics
372: 
373: **BAD:**
374: > "- Uses a custom font with negative letter spacing for a modern look"
375: 
376: **GOOD:**
377: > "- Geist Sans with extreme negative letter-spacing (-2.4px to -2.88px at display) -- text as compressed infrastructure"
378: 
379: **Why the good version works:** Names the font, gives the exact range, and the back-half metaphor ("compressed infrastructure") tells you the design intent in four words.
380: 
381: ---
382: 
383: ### 4. Do Entry
384: 
385: **BAD:**
386: > "- Use the correct colors for your design"
387: 
388: **GOOD:**
389: > "- Use `#171717` instead of `#000000` for primary text -- the micro-warmth matters"
390: 
391: **Why the good version works:** Names both the correct value and the common mistake. A developer who reads this will never accidentally use pure black.
392: 
393: ---
394: 
395: ### 5. Don't Entry
396: 
397: **BAD:**
398: > "- Don't use too many font weights"
399: 
400: **GOOD:**
401: > "- Don't use weight 700 (bold) on body text -- 600 is the maximum, used only for headings"
402: 
403: **Why the good version works:** Gives the exact prohibited weight, the exact maximum allowed weight, and the scope of the rule (body text vs. headings). A developer knows exactly what to check.
404: 
405: ---
406: 
407: ### 6. Component Documentation
408: 
409: **BAD:**
410: > "Cards have a white background with subtle shadows and rounded corners for a polished appearance."
411: 
412: **GOOD:**
413: > "Cards use white background with no CSS border. Shadow stack: `rgba(0,0,0,0.08) 0px 0px 0px 1px, rgba(0,0,0,0.04) 0px 2px 2px, #fafafa 0px 0px 0px 1px`. Radius 8px. Title at 24px Geist weight 600, letter-spacing -0.96px. Body at 16px weight 400, `#4d4d4d`."
414: 
415: **Why the good version works:** Every value is present. A developer can build this card from this description alone without looking at anything else.
416: 
417: ---
418: 
419: ### 7. Typography Note
420: 
421: **BAD:**
422: > "The typography creates a nice hierarchy with different sizes and weights that guide the user through the content."
423: 
424: **GOOD:**
425: > "Three weights, strict roles: 400 (body/reading), 500 (UI/interactive), 600 (headings/emphasis). No bold (700) except for tiny micro-badges. This narrow weight range creates hierarchy through size and tracking, not weight."
426: 
427: **Why the good version works:** Names every weight, assigns each weight a role, states the exception, and explains the architectural principle (hierarchy through size/tracking, not weight).
428: 
429: ---
430: 
431: ### 8. Layout Description
432: 
433: **BAD:**
434: > "The layout uses generous whitespace for a clean, breathable feel with well-organized content sections."
435: 
436: **GOOD:**
437: > "Gallery emptiness: massive vertical padding between sections (80px-120px+). The white space IS the design. Compressed text with aggressive negative letter-spacing on headlines is counterbalanced by vast surrounding whitespace. Section separation comes from borders and spacing alone -- no color variation between sections."
438: 
439: **Why the good version works:** Gives the exact padding range, names the technique ("gallery emptiness"), describes the tension between compressed text and expanded space, and states what is NOT used (no color variation) which is equally important.
440: 
441: ---
442: 
443: ### 9. Agent Prompt Guide
444: 
445: **BAD:**
446: > "Create a card component using the design system's colors, typography, and spacing. It should look like the rest of the site."
447: 
448: **GOOD:**
449: > "Design a card: white background, 1px solid #e5edf5 border, 6px radius. Shadow: rgba(50,50,93,0.25) 0px 30px 45px -30px, rgba(0,0,0,0.1) 0px 18px 36px -18px. Title at 22px sohne-var weight 300, letter-spacing -0.22px, color #061b31, 'ss01'. Body at 16px weight 300, #64748d."
450: 
451: **Why the good version works:** Every single value needed to build the card is present. The AI tool receiving this prompt has zero ambiguity about any visual property.
452: 
453: ---
454: 
455: ### 10. Section Opening
456: 
457: **BAD:**
458: > "In this section, we'll explore the depth and elevation system used throughout the design. Shadows play an important role in creating visual hierarchy."
459: 
460: **GOOD:**
461: > "Stripe's shadow system is built on a principle of chromatic depth. Where most design systems use neutral gray or black shadows, Stripe's primary shadow color (`rgba(50,50,93,0.25)`) is a deep blue-gray that echoes the brand's navy palette."
462: 
463: **Why the good version works:** No throat-clearing. Immediately states the principle (chromatic depth), names the specific technique (blue-tinted shadows), gives the exact value, and contrasts with the conventional approach.
464: 
465: ---
466: 
467: ## 12. SHADOW PHILOSOPHY PATTERN
468: 
469: Every DESIGN.md should include a shadow philosophy paragraph. This paragraph answers: "What is the THEORY behind this system's shadow usage?"
470: 
471: ### Structure
472: 
473: 1. Name the principle (chromatic depth, shadow-as-border, luminance stepping)
474: 2. Contrast with the conventional approach
475: 3. Explain the architectural benefit
476: 4. Provide 1-2 specific values as evidence
477: 
478: ### Example
479: 
480: > "Vercel has arguably the most sophisticated shadow system in modern web design. Rather than using shadows for elevation in the traditional Material Design sense, Vercel uses multi-value shadow stacks where each layer has a distinct architectural purpose: one creates the 'border' (0px spread, 1px), another adds ambient softness (2px blur), another handles depth at distance (8px blur with negative spread), and an inner ring (`#fafafa`) creates the subtle highlight that makes the card 'glow' from within."
481: 
482: ---
483: 
484: ## 13. SECTION STRUCTURE CHECKLIST (v3 Style Reference)
485: 
486: The v3 section set and where the prose effort goes. Pre-rendered sections are pasted unchanged; your writing is the prose in the remaining rows. Full contract: `design-md-format.md`.
487: 
488: | Section | Source | Density Target |
489: |---------|--------|----------------|
490: | Header + intro | prose | Tagline phrase + 4-6 grounded sentences |
491: | `## Tokens — Colors` | pre-rendered | (do not edit — named Name/Value/Token/Role table) |
492: | `## Tokens — Typography` | prose + facts | Per-font block + semantic Type Scale table |
493: | `## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes` | pre-rendered | (do not edit) |
494: | `## Components` | prose | Named components, every value present per component |
495: | `## Do's and Don'ts` | prose | Each bullet cites a concrete value and reads as an instruction |
496: | `## Surfaces` | pre-rendered | (do not edit) |
497: | `## Elevation` | prose | Shadow list, or one honest "flat" line when 0 shadows |
498: | `## Imagery` | prose | Grounded treatment, or ABSENT when no imagery signal |
499: | `## Layout` | prose | Max-width, rhythm, nav — grounded in spacing/breakpoint data |
500: | `## Agent Prompt Guide` | prose | Quick Color Reference + 3-5 self-contained prompts |
501: | `## Similar Brands` | prose | 3-5 brands, one grounded-inference WHY each |
502: | `## Quick Start` | pre-rendered | (do not edit — CSS `:root` + Tailwind `@theme`) |
503: 
504: ---
505: 
506: ## 14. FINAL QUALITY GATE
507: 
508: Before publishing a Style Reference, run these checks:
509: 
510: - [ ] Tagline passes the "could this describe three other sites?" test -- NO
511: - [ ] Zero banned words in descriptive prose
512: - [ ] Intro paragraph (4-6 sentences) has every claim mapped to a real value
513: - [ ] Colours are NAMED evocatively; every name maps to a `--color-<slug>` token; no `--_color-primitives` var leaked
514: - [ ] Components are NAMED by function (Primary CTA, Card, Badge) — no "Variant-N" or "div"
515: - [ ] Values are embedded in prose (not standalone facts) in narrative sections
516: - [ ] Values are standalone and scannable in the pre-rendered tables and component specs
517: - [ ] Every Do/Don't cites a concrete value and reads as an instruction
518: - [ ] Every agent prompt is self-contained (copy-paste ready, no doc lookups)
519: - [ ] No transition phrases ("let's look at," "in this section")
520: - [ ] No frequency dumps in prose — frequency decides prominence, it is never printed
521: - [ ] Elevation is honest: "flat" stated plainly when 0 shadows, never dressed up as "gradient-as-depth"
522: - [ ] No false SYSTEM asserted (no "focus is consistent" when the data says otherwise)
523: - [ ] Pre-rendered sections (Colors, Spacing & Shapes, Surfaces, Quick Start) pasted UNCHANGED
524: - [ ] Information density: no sentence survives the deletion test without losing information
525: 
526: ---
527: 
528: ## 15. COMPARATIVE FRAMING PATTERN
529: 
530: Comparative framing is useful ONLY when it compares elements WITHIN this system using extracted values. Do NOT compare to "most systems", "convention", or "the typical approach" -- `tokens.json` carries no data about other systems, so those claims are fabrication. (This pattern previously produced ungrounded "unlike most systems" sentences; keep comparisons intra-system.)
531: 
532: ### Sentence templates (intra-system only)
533: 
534: - "The H1 (-2.4px tracking) is tighter than body (0px) -- compression scales with size"
535: - "Cards use a 7px radius while buttons use 10.5px -- the system distinguishes containers from controls"
536: - "This is not the [common thing]; it is [the specific thing]"
537: - "The conventional choice would be X; here, Y signals [intent]"
538: - "Rather than defaulting to X, the system [specific verb] Y"
539: 
540: ### Good/Bad example pairs
541: 
542: **1. Shadow philosophy**
543: 
544: BAD: "The system uses subtle shadows for depth."
545: 
546: GOOD: "Where most systems use neutral gray shadows, this system tints its elevation shadows with brand navy (`rgba(50,50,93,0.25)`), creating chromatic depth rather than flat Material-style layering."
547: 
548: **2. Typography weight**
549: 
550: BAD: "Headlines use a light weight for a refined look."
551: 
552: GOOD: "Unlike the convention of bold (700) headlines that shout for attention, this system uses weight 300 at display sizes -- whispered authority that trusts its content to carry the page."
553: 
554: **3. Border technique**
555: 
556: BAD: "Borders are implemented with box-shadow."
557: 
558: GOOD: "This is not a traditional CSS border; it is a zero-blur box-shadow (`0 0 0 1px rgba(0,0,0,0.08)`) that achieves a border-like hairline without participating in the box model, preventing the 1px layout shifts that CSS borders cause."
559: 
560: **4. Color palette**
561: 
562: BAD: "The color palette is mostly neutral with one accent."
563: 
564: GOOD: "Rather than the typical SaaS approach of warm gray neutrals with a blue CTA, this system commits to a true achromatic neutral scale (`#171717` to `#fafafa`) and reserves all chromaticity for a single accent (`#5e6ad2`), making every colored pixel a deliberate signal."
565: 
566: **5. Spacing**
567: 
568: BAD: "The system uses generous whitespace."
569: 
570: GOOD: "The conventional 40-60px section spacing would feel timid here. At 80-120px between sections, the whitespace IS the design -- gallery-like emptiness that frames compressed, tightly-tracked headlines as precious objects."
571: 
572: **6. Button design**
573: 
574: BAD: "Buttons have a minimal style."
575: 
576: GOOD: "Where most design systems give buttons solid backgrounds and obvious affordance, this system builds buttons from near-transparent overlays (`rgba(255,255,255,0.04)`) -- the button is barely there until hover reveals it, trusting the user to recognize interactive patterns."
577: 
578: ### When to use comparative framing
579: 
580: - Opening paragraphs (1-2 comparisons max)
581: - Shadow philosophy paragraph
582: - Typography principles section
583: - Any key characteristic that contradicts convention
584: - Do's and Don'ts entries where the "Don't" IS the convention
585: 
586: ---
587: 
588: ## 16. NAMED PRINCIPLE PATTERN
589: 
590: Name a design decision ONLY when extracted tokens back it (cite the value). A named principle without backing data is fabrication -- this pattern previously produced "gradient-as-depth" from a site with zero shadow tokens. When the data supports no distinctive principle, omit the name; do not invent one to fill the section.
591: 
592: ### Naming formula
593: 
594: **Pattern A:** [adjective] + [noun]
595: **Pattern B:** [technique]-as-[metaphor]
596: **Pattern C:** [quality] + [domain]
597: 
598: ### 10+ examples across design domains
599: 
600: **Color:**
601: - **Chromatic depth** -- shadows tinted with brand hue rather than neutral black
602: - **Achromatic commitment** -- zero chromatic color in the neutral scale; all saturation reserved for accents
603: - **Single-hue discipline** -- one accent hue across the entire system; no secondary chromatic colors
604: 
605: **Typography:**
606: - **Whispered authority** -- headline weight 300 at display sizes; light weight as signature
607: - **Compressed infrastructure** -- extreme negative letter-spacing (-2.4px+) that makes text feel minified for production
608: - **Bilingual parallelism** -- dual-language text set with identical visual weight and spacing regardless of script
609: 
610: **Shadow:**
611: - **Shadow-as-border** -- zero-blur box-shadow replaces CSS border throughout the system
612: - **Ambient occlusion** -- individual shadow layers never exceeding 0.05 opacity; light that feels natural rather than rendered
613: - **Parallax depth** -- multi-layer shadow stacks where tinted and neutral layers sit at different offsets
614: 
615: **Layout:**
616: - **Gallery emptiness** -- section spacing exceeding 80px; whitespace as the primary design element
617: - **Content density polarity** -- compressed text set against vast surrounding whitespace; the tension IS the layout
618: 
619: **Interaction:**
620: - **Transparency-first affordance** -- interactive elements built from near-zero opacity overlays; the component reveals itself on hover
621: - **Light weight as signature** -- the system's identity is defined by what it does NOT do (no bold, no heavy shadows, no solid backgrounds)
622: 
623: ### How to introduce a named principle
624: 
625: Introduce it in the prose where the observation first appears, then reference it by name in later sections:
626: 
627: > "Stripe's shadow system is built on a principle of **chromatic depth**: where most systems use neutral gray or black shadows, Stripe's primary shadow color (`rgba(50,50,93,0.25)`) is a deep blue-gray that echoes the brand's navy palette."
628: 
629: Later: "The card shadow follows the **chromatic depth** principle established in the elevation section."
630: 
631: ---
632: 
633: ## 17. FREQUENCY IS A DECISION INPUT, NEVER DISPLAYED
634: 
635: Frequency DECIDES prominence and role — which colour is the primary, which is a rare accent, which radius is the default. It is never PRINTED. The v3 Style Reference shows no counts, no percentages, no "appears 9685 times" narration. Frequency informs the ordering and the role clauses; it never becomes a sentence.
636: 
637: ### How frequency informs (silently)
638: 
639: | Frequency tier | What it decides | How it shows up |
640: |---|---|---|
641: | Dominant | This is the system default / primary | Ordered first in the pre-rendered table; role clause says "primary text" or "canvas" |
642: | Common | Supporting structural role | Mid-table; role clause names the structural use ("borders", "card surfaces") |
643: | Moderate / Rare | Intentional accent, reserved signal | Lower in the table; role clause adds a usage guard ("interactive elements only") |
644: | Absent in expected role | A deliberate omission worth stating | A Do/Don't or an honest "flat" / "no distinct CTA color" line |
645: 
646: ### Good — frequency expressed as ROLE, not number
647: 
648: > Voltage (`#06458c`) — interactive elements only; do not promote it to a static text colour.
649: 
650: > The system has two radii: 7px on buttons, 14px on cards — controls and containers are distinguished by corner, not fill.
651: 
652: ### Bad — frequency leaked as a number
653: 
654: > "`#171717` accounts for 62% of text usage." (Frequency dump — say "primary text" instead.)
655: 
656: > "The `0 0 0 1px` shadow appears 4x more often than any elevation shadow." (Count printed — characterize the role, not the tally.)
657: 
658: ### Stating a deliberate absence
659: 
660: An absence can still be stated — as a fact about the system, never as a frequency figure:
661: 
662: > Do not add `box-shadow` — there are zero shadow tokens; any shadow is an invention. Depth here is carried by border contrast and whitespace.
663: 
664: ---
665: 
666: ## 18. INTENT NARRATION PATTERN
667: 
668: Intent narration bridges the gap between WHAT a system does and WHY it does it. Every design decision is a choice among alternatives; intent narration names the road not taken.
669: 
670: ### Sentence templates
671: 
672: - "The system uses X because Y"
673: - "[Value] at [context] signals [meaning]"
674: - "This choice trades [sacrifice] for [benefit]"
675: - "X over Y because [rationale]"
676: - "[Observation] -- a deliberate trade of [cost] for [gain]"
677: 
678: ### 5+ examples
679: 
680: > "Weight 510 sits between regular (400) and medium (500) -- a micro-emphasis that creates distinction without the visual interruption of a full weight jump. The system trades conventional weight stops for in-between precision."
681: 
682: > "`#171717` instead of `#000000` for primary text signals a system that values reading comfort over maximum contrast. The 2% lightness shift is invisible in isolation but measurable across 2000 words of body copy."
683: 
684: > "Individual shadow layer opacity never exceeds 0.05 -- the system chooses ambient realism over Material-style elevation theatrics. The shadows feel like natural light rather than computer-generated depth."
685: 
686: > "Letter-spacing of -2.4px at display sizes compresses character width by roughly 8%, creating text that feels like infrastructure -- minified, efficient, engineered. The system trades readability at glance for density of meaning."
687: 
688: > "Section padding at 96px vertical when the conventional range is 40-60px -- the system spends screen real estate on emptiness, signaling that the content within each section is complete and self-contained rather than a continuous scroll."
689: 
690: ### Intent narration test
691: 
692: Ask: "Does this sentence tell me something I could not infer from looking at the CSS value alone?" If no, the sentence is observation without intent. Add the WHY.
693: 
694: ---
695: 
696: ## 19. BRAND VOICE DETECTION PATTERN
697: 
698: When the extracted data includes `sampleTexts` from tokens.json, UI text from buttons, headings, and labels, or microcopy from forms and errors, these are signals of the brand's content voice.
699: 
700: ### How to infer tone from sampleTexts
701: 
702: 1. **Sentence length**: Short, punchy sentences (3-5 words) signal directness and confidence. Long, qualified sentences signal formality or caution.
703: 2. **Punctuation**: Exclamation marks suggest enthusiasm or consumer-facing energy. Periods-only suggests restraint. Em-dashes and semicolons suggest editorial sophistication.
704: 3. **Person**: "You/your" signals conversational, user-centric voice. "We" signals partnership. Absence of pronouns signals institutional formality.
705: 4. **Jargon density**: Technical terms without explanation signal expert audience. Explained terms signal broader audience.
706: 
707: ### How to detect casing conventions from button labels
708: 
709: | Observed pattern | Convention name | Brand signal |
710: |---|---|---|
711: | "Get Started" | Title Case | Traditional, corporate, formal |
712: | "Get started" | Sentence case | Modern, approachable, lowercase-friendly |
713: | "GET STARTED" | All caps | Commanding, urgent, action-oriented |
714: | "get started" | All lowercase | Ultra-casual, startup, counter-cultural |
715: | "はじめる" / "始める" | Localized verb | Japanese-native, not translated |
716: 
717: ### How to identify emoji policy
718: 
719: - **Emojis in headings or buttons**: Consumer-facing, playful, younger demographic
720: - **Emojis in body text only**: Light personality injection, still professional
721: - **Emojis in documentation/help**: Approachable support tone
722: - **Zero emojis anywhere**: Formal, enterprise, or conservative brand -- document this as a deliberate absence
723: - **Emoji as icon substitute**: Functional, not decorative (e.g., checkmark emoji replacing an icon)
724: 
725: ### How to distinguish formal vs informal voice
726: 
727: | Signal | Formal | Informal |
728: |---|---|---|
729: | Contractions | "do not", "cannot" | "don't", "can't" |
730: | Error messages | "An error has occurred" | "Something went wrong" |
731: | Empty states | "No results found" | "Nothing here yet" |
732: | Button text | "Submit Request" | "Send it" |
733: | Success messages | "Operation completed successfully" | "Done!" |
734: 
735: ### Documentation format
736: 
737: In the DESIGN.md Content & Voice section:
738: 
739: ```markdown
740: ## Content & Voice
741: 
742: **Tone**: [adjective], [adjective], [adjective] (e.g., "precise, restrained, institutional")
743: **Casing**: [Sentence case / Title Case / ALL CAPS] on buttons and headings
744: **Emoji policy**: [None / Functional only / Decorative in body / Throughout]
745: **Person**: [Second person "you" / First person plural "we" / Impersonal]
746: **Sample voice**: "[exact button text]", "[exact heading]", "[exact error message]"
747: ```
748: 
749: ---
750: 
751: ## 20. SELF-CONTAINMENT CHECKLIST (Agent Prompt Guide)
752: 
753: Every agent prompt must be fully self-contained. The test: "Can an AI agent copy-paste this prompt and build the component with zero lookups into the rest of the DESIGN.md?"
754: 
755: ### Required values in every prompt
756: 
757: - [ ] Font family name (exact string, e.g., `"Inter"`, `"sohne-var"`)
758: - [ ] Font size in px
759: - [ ] Font weight as numeric value
760: - [ ] Line-height (unitless ratio or px)
761: - [ ] Letter-spacing (px or em, including `0` if default)
762: - [ ] All hex color values for every element (background, text, border, icon)
763: - [ ] Padding (all sides, shorthand or explicit)
764: - [ ] Border-radius in px
765: - [ ] Box-shadow (full CSS value or `none`)
766: - [ ] Transition (property, duration, easing)
767: - [ ] OpenType features if the system uses them (`ss01`, `cv01`, etc.)
768: - [ ] Border (width, style, color) or explicit `none`
769: 
770: ### Self-containment test
771: 
772: 1. Copy the prompt into a blank AI chat
773: 2. Ask: "Build this component"
774: 3. If the AI asks a clarifying question about any visual property, the prompt fails
775: 4. If the AI guesses any value (defaulting to `border-radius: 8px` because no radius was specified), the prompt fails
776: 
777: ### Failure examples and fixes
778: 
779: **FAILS**: "Create a button with the primary brand color" -- which color?
780: **PASSES**: "Create a button with background `#5e6ad2`, text `#ffffff`"
781: 
782: **FAILS**: "Use the system font at heading size" -- which font, which size?
783: **PASSES**: "Use Inter at 32px weight 600 line-height 1.2 letter-spacing -0.96px"
784: 
785: **FAILS**: "Add the standard card shadow" -- what is standard?
786: **PASSES**: "Add shadow `0 1px 3px rgba(0,0,0,0.06), 0 0 0 1px rgba(0,0,0,0.08)`"

16: ---
17: # DESIGN.md Writing Style Guide
18: 
19: Writing quality standard for the v3 **Style Reference** output (see `design-md-format.md`). This guide governs the prose voice only — named and restrained, not mechanical and hedged.
20: 
21: ---
22: 
23: ## 1. OVERVIEW
24: 
25: The Style Reference is a named, role-driven, ship-ready design-system handoff — not an extraction report. Every value still traces verbatim to `tokens.json`. Write like a design-systems lead handing the system off to the team that will ship it tomorrow. The reader already knows CSS, typography, and color theory -- never explain fundamentals.
26: 
27: **Division of labour (read this first).** In the v3 pipeline the value-bearing sections — `## Tokens — Colors`, `## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes`, `## Surfaces`, and `## Quick Start` — are pre-rendered deterministically by `backend/scripts/formatters-v3.ts` (a hue+lightness colour-namer and emitters) and pasted into the doc unchanged. The agent writes **prose only** (header, intro, Typography role prose, Components, Do's/Don'ts, Elevation, Imagery, Layout, Agent Prompt Guide, Similar Brands). You never hand-author a value table, so "100rem where the tokens say 100%" cannot happen — this guide is about making the prose worthy of the named tokens, not about transcribing numbers.
28: 
29: **Voice characteristics — named, confident, restrained:**
30: - **Named.** Colours, components, and surfaces carry evocative, grounded names (Obsidian Ink, Voltage, Primary CTA, Canvas), never "Color 1" or "Variant-1". Naming is a grounded inference about hue, lightness, and role — it is allowed and expected.
31: - **Confident.** State roles plainly and assign Similar Brands as grounded inference. Do not hedge every sentence with "appears to" or "seems". You are characterizing what IS there.
32: - **Restrained.** One grounded clause, not a paragraph of metaphor. "A warm-tinted near-black" beats "letters like hull plates." No purple prose.
33: - **Honest.** Confident never means inventing a SYSTEM the data contradicts. No "gradient-as-depth" with 0 shadow tokens, no "focus is consistent" when `focusIndicator.consistent` is false. Name and characterize what exists; never assert a relationship the tokens deny.
34: - **Dense, not noisy.** Every sentence carries one piece of implementation-changing information. But never dump raw mechanics: no frequency counts ("border 9685, text 4258"), no extractor-internal var names (`--_color-primitives---neutral--1400`), no DOM-tag labels ("div"). Frequency DECIDES prominence and role; it is never printed.
35: 
36: **Audience model:** A frontend engineer absorbing the system before building a component. Do NOT assume a market audience the page never states ("targets captains and port agents") — characterize the design, not an imagined user.
37: 
38: ---
39: 
40: ## 2. BANNED WORDS
41: 
42: NEVER use these words in descriptive prose. They communicate nothing specific and signal that the writer ran out of things to observe:
43: 
44: `clean`, `modern`, `sleek`, `professional`, `user-friendly`, `intuitive`, `elegant`, `beautiful`, `stunning`, `gorgeous`, `polished`, `refined`, `sophisticated`, `seamless`, `cutting-edge`, `state-of-the-art`, `next-generation`, `innovative`, `revolutionary`, `world-class`, `premium` (when used as a vague adjective rather than a pricing tier), `crisp`, `delightful`, `lovely`, `nice`, `simple` (when used approvingly without specifics)
45: 
46: **The replacement rule:** Every banned word is a placeholder for a specific observation you have not yet made. Find the observation.
47: 
48: | Banned phrase | What to write instead |
49: |---|---|
50: | "clean design" | "gallery-like emptiness where section padding exceeds 80px and the only color signal comes from three workflow-specific accents" |
51: | "modern typography" | "Inter Variable at weight 510 with OpenType `cv01` and `ss03` -- a between-weight that creates emphasis without the heaviness of traditional medium" |
52: | "sleek interface" | "near-black canvas (`#08090a`) where content emerges through four luminance steps of semi-transparent white backgrounds" |
53: | "professional color palette" | "achromatic system with a single chromatic accent (`#5e6ad2`) reserved exclusively for interactive elements" |
54: | "intuitive layout" | "single-column hero with 80-120px vertical padding, collapsing to 2-3 column card grids at the feature section level" |
55: | "elegant shadows" | "multi-layer shadow stacks where blue-tinted `rgba(50,50,93,0.25)` sits at 30px offset while neutral `rgba(0,0,0,0.1)` sits closer at 18px, creating parallax depth" |
56: 
57: ---
58: 
59: ## 3. HEADER — TAGLINE RULES
60: 
61: The header is a title line, an evocative `> tagline`, and a `**Theme:**` line:
62: 
63: ```
64: # <Brand or Domain> — Style Reference
65: > <one-line evocative tagline — the design's essence in a phrase>
66: 
67: **Theme:** light | dark | mixed
68: ```
69: 
70: The **tagline** is a single grounded, evocative phrase. It must do three things simultaneously:
71: 
72: 1. **Capture the design system's essence** -- not its parameters, but its character and position
73: 2. **Use a precise framing** that makes this system distinguishable from every other
74: 3. **Let a reader who has never seen the site form a mental image** that would survive comparison with the real thing
75: 
76: ### What the tagline is NOT
77: 
78: - A parameter list: "Uses Inter font, dark backgrounds, and purple accents."
79: - A compliment or banned word: "A beautifully designed, modern system."
80: - A bare category label: "A minimalist dark-mode design system."
81: - An invented fact about the brand or its audience.
82: 
83: ### What the tagline IS
84: 
85: An essence capture -- one phrase that makes someone say "I know exactly what this looks like." It characterizes; it never fabricates a fact.
86: 
87: ### Example taglines
88: 
89: > Broadsheet financial broadside — the masthead itself is the design
90: 
91: > A near-black canvas where content emerges through four luminance steps
92: 
93: > Developer infrastructure made invisible — restraint as a thesis
94: 
95: ### Tagline test
96: 
97: Ask: "Could this phrase describe three other sites?" If yes, it fails. A tagline must be so specific that swapping it onto a different site would feel wrong.
98: 
99: ---
100: 
101: ## 4. INTRO PARAGRAPH
102: 
103: Directly under the header, one unlabeled paragraph of **4-6 sentences**. It characterizes the system's voice across these dimensions: the canvas, the dominant type move, how colour is rationed, layout density, and what carries the page. Every characterizing claim must map to a real token (a hex, a size, a weight). Restrained, not purple. No assumed audience unless the page states it.
104: 
105: > "The canvas is a warm-tinted near-black (`#121613`), with Obsidian Ink doing double duty as text, borders, and image frames. A single high-voltage accent (`#06458c`) is rationed strictly to interactive elements — everything else is neutral by default. Display type runs at 140px with -1.4px tracking against a 16px body, so hierarchy comes from scale, not weight. Section rhythm is spacious: large gaps frame each block as self-contained. The system is flat — no shadow tokens — and depth is carried by border contrast and whitespace alone."
106: 
107: Note: every claim cites a real value, colours are named (Obsidian Ink, the accent), the flat-elevation truth is stated plainly rather than dressed up as "gradient-as-depth", and there is no invented audience.
108: 
109: ### Intro test
110: 
111: Each sentence should be deletable without making the others incomprehensible, but their combined effect is a complete picture: canvas → type → colour rationing → layout → what carries depth. A sentence with zero values is an opinion — cut it or ground it.
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 5. KEY CHARACTERISTICS FORMAT
116: 
117: Each key characteristic follows a strict two-part structure joined by an em-dash:
118: 
119: ```
120: - [Design intent / what it achieves] -- [implementation parameters / how to do it]
121: ```
122: 
123: The front half tells you WHY. The back half tells you WHAT. Neither half works alone.
124: 
125: ### Good key characteristics
126: 
127: ```
128: - Geist Sans with extreme negative letter-spacing (-2.4px to -2.88px at display) -- text as compressed infrastructure
129: - Shadow-as-border technique: `box-shadow 0px 0px 0px 1px` replaces traditional borders throughout
130: - Weight 300 as the signature headline weight -- light, confident, anti-convention
131: - Dark-mode-native: `#08090a` marketing background, `#0f1011` panel background, `#191a1b` elevated surfaces
132: ```
133: 
134: ### Bad key characteristics
135: 
136: ```
137: - Uses a nice dark color palette (no values, no contrast, "nice" is banned)
138: - The font is Inter (no weight, no features, no personality)
139: - Has good spacing (no values, no philosophy)
140: - Borders are thin (how thin? what technique? why?)
141: ```
142: 
143: ### Quantity
144: 
145: 8-12 key characteristics. Fewer means you missed something. More means you are listing parameters instead of characteristics. A characteristic is a parameter + its design significance.
146: 
147: ---
148: 
149: ## 6. COLOUR NAMING (`## Tokens — Colors`)
150: 
151: In v3 the colour table is **pre-rendered** by `formatters-v3.ts` in the `Name | Value | Token | Role` shape, most-prominent first. You do not hand-author it — but you must understand the naming style, because the Quick Start re-uses these exact slugs and the rest of your prose references colours by their names.
152: 
153: ```
154: | Name | Value | Token | Role |
155: |------|-------|-------|------|
156: | Obsidian Ink | `#121613` | `--color-obsidian-ink` | Primary text, borders, image frames — a warm-tinted near-black |
157: | Voltage | `#06458c` | `--color-voltage` | Interactive elements only — do not promote it to a static text colour |
158: ```
159: 
160: Each column has a job:
161: 
162: 1. **Name** — evocative + grounded (hue + lightness + character). Neutrals by lightness (Snow/Linen → Ink/Obsidian/Void); hued by family + character (Voltage/Azure/Ember/Sage/Mist). Be consistent within a doc.
163: 2. **Value** — 6-digit lowercase hex, verbatim. Gradients render their full `linear-gradient(...)` value.
164: 3. **Token** — `--color-<kebab-name>` derived from the Name. NEVER the extractor's internal `--_color-primitives` var.
165: 4. **Role** — where it is used (grounded in measured usage) plus one characterizing clause. No frequency numbers. For a supporting accent, add a usage guard ("Do not promote it to the primary CTA color").
166: 
167: ### Good role clauses
168: 
169: > Primary text, borders, image frames — a warm-tinted near-black
170: 
171: > Card surfaces — same hex as canvas, so cards are defined by radius and padding, not fill
172: 
173: ### Bad role clauses
174: 
175: > Used for buttons. (No character, no usage guard)
176: 
177: > The colour that appears 9685 times. (Frequency dump — frequency decides prominence, it is never printed)
178: 
179: > `--_color-primitives---neutral--1400`. (Extractor-internal var leaked into the token column)
180: 
181: ### The characterizing clause
182: 
183: It describes visual quality, not emotional reaction, and never restates the hex in words. "A warm-tinted near-black" tells you something measurable. "Beautiful dark colour" does not. L1/L2 colours go in the main table; L3 in a `### Current Campaign Colors (Subject to change)` sub-table; L4 is excluded entirely.
184: 
185: ---
186: 
187: ## 7. VALUE EMBEDDING
188: 
189: Design values (font sizes, letter-spacing, weights, hex codes, opacity values) must be woven into prose. They never stand alone as facts.
190: 
191: ### The rule
192: 
193: A value without context is a spec sheet entry. A value inside a sentence that explains its effect is design documentation.
194: 
195: ### Good value embedding
196: 
197: > "The aggressive negative letter-spacing (-2.4px at display sizes) creates text that feels minified for production."
198: 
199: > "The 510 weight sits between regular and medium, creating a subtle emphasis that doesn't shout."
200: 
201: > "Individual shadow layer opacity never exceeds 0.05, producing ambient occlusion that feels like natural light rather than computer-generated depth."
202: 
203: ### Bad value embedding
204: 
205: > "Letter spacing: -2.4px. This creates compression."
206: 
207: Two sentences where one would do. The value and its effect are separated, making the reader do assembly work.
208: 
209: > "The letter-spacing is -2.4px."
210: 
211: A fact with no consequence. Why should someone care that it is -2.4px? What does -2.4px produce that -1px or -0.5px does not?
212: 
213: > "Font size: 48px, Weight: 600, Line height: 1.00, Letter spacing: -2.4px"
214: 
215: A parameter dump. This belongs in a table, not in prose. Prose exists to explain what tables cannot: the relationships between parameters and the reasons behind choices.
216: 
217: ### Where values DO stand alone
218: 
219: Tables, component specs, and agent prompt guides. These are reference contexts where scanability matters more than narrative. In those contexts, every value should be present and findable. In prose sections, values are evidence for claims.
220: 
221: ---
222: 
223: ## 8. DO'S AND DON'TS QUALITY
224: 
225: The Do's and Don'ts section is where most DESIGN.md files fail. Generic advice wastes the reader's time. Every entry must pass the specificity test.
226: 
227: ### Don'ts: The Counter-Intuitive Test
228: 
229: A good Don't tells the reader something they would naturally do that is WRONG in this specific system. It should surprise someone who knows CSS and design but does not know this particular system.
230: 
231: **Each Don't needs three components:**
232: 1. What not to do
233: 2. Why it is wrong in THIS system (not in general)
234: 3. What to do instead (with at least one specific value)
235: 
236: ### Good Don'ts
237: 
238: > "Don't use weight 600-700 for sohne-var headlines -- weight 300 is the brand voice"
239: 
240: Counter-intuitive: most systems use heavy weights for headlines. The reader would default to 600+ without this warning.
241: 
242: > "Don't skip the inner `#fafafa` ring in card shadows -- it's the glow that makes the elevation system work"
243: 
244: Counter-intuitive: a developer building a card shadow would include the obvious layers (border, elevation) and skip the inner ring because it seems decorative. This Don't explains that it is structural.
245: 
246: > "Don't use solid colored backgrounds for buttons -- transparency is the system (rgba white at 0.02-0.05)"
247: 
248: Counter-intuitive: every instinct says to give buttons a solid background color. Linear's system is built on near-zero opacity.
249: 
250: ### Bad Don'ts
251: 
252: > "Don't use too many colors"
253: 
254: No threshold, no alternative, applicable to every design system ever created.
255: 
256: > "Don't forget accessibility"
257: 
258: Not a design system rule. This is a general web development principle.
259: 
260: > "Don't make things too large"
261: 
262: Too large relative to what? No values, no system-specific context.
263: 
264: ### Do's: The Implementation Shortcut Test
265: 
266: A good Do gives a reader an implementation shortcut. After reading it, they should be able to write correct CSS faster.
267: 
268: ### Good Do's
269: 
270: > "Use shadow-as-border (`0px 0px 0px 1px rgba(0,0,0,0.08)`) instead of traditional CSS borders"
271: 
272: Gives the exact value and names the technique. A developer can copy this into their code immediately.
273: 
274: > "Use `#171717` instead of `#000000` for primary text -- the micro-warmth matters"
275: 
276: Names both the correct value AND the common mistake, with a one-phrase rationale.
277: 
278: ---
279: 
280: ## 9. AGENT PROMPT GUIDE
281: 
282: Agent prompts must be SELF-CONTAINED. A developer copies one prompt into an AI tool and gets a correct component without needing the rest of the DESIGN.md.
283: 
284: ### Requirements
285: 
286: - **Complete hex values** for every color mentioned
287: - **Font family, size, weight, and line-height** for every text element
288: - **Letter-spacing** where the system uses non-default tracking
289: - **Padding, radius, and shadow values** for every container or interactive element
290: - **OpenType features** if the system uses them
291: - **100-200 words each** -- long enough to be complete, short enough to fit in a prompt window
292: 
293: ### Good agent prompt
294: 
295: > "Create a hero section on white background. Headline at 48px Geist weight 600, line-height 1.00, letter-spacing -2.4px, color #171717. Subtitle at 20px Geist weight 400, line-height 1.80, color #4d4d4d. Dark CTA button (#171717, 6px radius, 8px 16px padding) and ghost button (white, shadow-border rgba(0,0,0,0.08) 0px 0px 0px 1px, 6px radius)."
296: 
297: Every value is present. No lookups required.
298: 
299: ### Bad agent prompt
300: 
301: > "Create a hero section using the brand colors and primary font. Make the headline large and the subtitle smaller. Add a primary and secondary button."
302: 
303: Every value is missing. The AI tool would guess, and every guess would be wrong.
304: 
305: ### Prompt coverage
306: 
307: Include prompts for at least:
308: - Hero section
309: - Card component
310: - Badge/pill
311: - Navigation
312: - One system-specific component (workflow pipeline, command palette, dark section)
313: 
314: ---
315: 
316: ## 10. INFORMATION DENSITY
317: 
318: ### The deletion test
319: 
320: Read every sentence. Ask: "If I delete this, does the reader lose implementation-relevant information?" If no, delete it.
321: 
322: ### Banned transition phrases
323: 
324: Never write:
325: - "Let's look at..."
326: - "In this section, we'll explore..."
327: - "Now let's move on to..."
328: - "As we can see..."
329: - "It's worth noting that..."
330: - "It's important to mention..."
331: - "Another key aspect is..."
332: 
333: These phrases exist in drafts. They do not exist in published technical writing. They add words without adding information.
334: 
335: ### No restating tables
336: 
337: If a value appears in a table, do not repeat it in the prose below the table unless the prose adds NEW information about that value (rationale, relationship to another value, historical context).
338: 
339: ### Paragraph density target
340: 
341: Each prose paragraph (intro, Typography role prose, Layout, Elevation) should contain 2-4 concrete values (hex codes, pixel values, weights, opacities). A paragraph with zero values is an opinion. A paragraph with one value is an observation. A paragraph with 2-4 values is documentation.
342: 
343: ---
344: 
345: ## 11. TEN GOOD/BAD WRITING COMPARISONS
346: 
347: ### 1. Atmosphere Description
348: 
349: **BAD:**
350: > "The website has a clean, modern design with a dark color scheme that looks very professional and sleek."
351: 
352: **GOOD:**
353: > "Linear's website is a masterclass in dark-mode-first product design -- a near-black canvas (`#08090a`) where content emerges from darkness like starlight. The overall impression is one of extreme precision engineering: every element exists in a carefully calibrated hierarchy of luminance, from barely-visible borders (`rgba(255,255,255,0.05)`) to soft, luminous text (`#f7f8f8`)."
354: 
355: **Why the good version works:** Three specific values, a metaphor that communicates visual quality ("starlight"), and a structural observation (luminance hierarchy) instead of a vague adjective.
356: 
357: ---
358: 
359: ### 2. Color Description
360: 
361: **BAD:**
362: > "The primary color is a nice shade of purple (#533afd) that is used for buttons and links."
363: 
364: **GOOD:**
365: > "**Stripe Purple** (`#533afd`): Primary brand color, CTA backgrounds, link text, interactive highlights. A saturated blue-violet that anchors the entire system. This isn't the cold, clinical purple of enterprise software; it's a rich, saturated violet that reads as confident."
366: 
367: **Why the good version works:** Names the color, lists all its roles (not just buttons), provides a personality sentence, and contrasts it with what it is NOT (cold, clinical enterprise purple).
368: 
369: ---
370: 
371: ### 3. Key Characteristics
372: 
373: **BAD:**
374: > "- Uses a custom font with negative letter spacing for a modern look"
375: 
376: **GOOD:**
377: > "- Geist Sans with extreme negative letter-spacing (-2.4px to -2.88px at display) -- text as compressed infrastructure"
378: 
379: **Why the good version works:** Names the font, gives the exact range, and the back-half metaphor ("compressed infrastructure") tells you the design intent in four words.
380: 
381: ---
382: 
383: ### 4. Do Entry
384: 
385: **BAD:**
386: > "- Use the correct colors for your design"
387: 
388: **GOOD:**
389: > "- Use `#171717` instead of `#000000` for primary text -- the micro-warmth matters"
390: 
391: **Why the good version works:** Names both the correct value and the common mistake. A developer who reads this will never accidentally use pure black.
392: 
393: ---
394: 
395: ### 5. Don't Entry
396: 
397: **BAD:**
398: > "- Don't use too many font weights"
399: 
400: **GOOD:**
401: > "- Don't use weight 700 (bold) on body text -- 600 is the maximum, used only for headings"
402: 
403: **Why the good version works:** Gives the exact prohibited weight, the exact maximum allowed weight, and the scope of the rule (body text vs. headings). A developer knows exactly what to check.
404: 
405: ---
406: 
407: ### 6. Component Documentation
408: 
409: **BAD:**
410: > "Cards have a white background with subtle shadows and rounded corners for a polished appearance."
411: 
412: **GOOD:**
413: > "Cards use white background with no CSS border. Shadow stack: `rgba(0,0,0,0.08) 0px 0px 0px 1px, rgba(0,0,0,0.04) 0px 2px 2px, #fafafa 0px 0px 0px 1px`. Radius 8px. Title at 24px Geist weight 600, letter-spacing -0.96px. Body at 16px weight 400, `#4d4d4d`."
414: 
415: **Why the good version works:** Every value is present. A developer can build this card from this description alone without looking at anything else.
416: 
417: ---
418: 
419: ### 7. Typography Note
420: 
421: **BAD:**
422: > "The typography creates a nice hierarchy with different sizes and weights that guide the user through the content."
423: 
424: **GOOD:**
425: > "Three weights, strict roles: 400 (body/reading), 500 (UI/interactive), 600 (headings/emphasis). No bold (700) except for tiny micro-badges. This narrow weight range creates hierarchy through size and tracking, not weight."
426: 
427: **Why the good version works:** Names every weight, assigns each weight a role, states the exception, and explains the architectural principle (hierarchy through size/tracking, not weight).
428: 
429: ---
430: 
431: ### 8. Layout Description
432: 
433: **BAD:**
434: > "The layout uses generous whitespace for a clean, breathable feel with well-organized content sections."
435: 
436: **GOOD:**
437: > "Gallery emptiness: massive vertical padding between sections (80px-120px+). The white space IS the design. Compressed text with aggressive negative letter-spacing on headlines is counterbalanced by vast surrounding whitespace. Section separation comes from borders and spacing alone -- no color variation between sections."
438: 
439: **Why the good version works:** Gives the exact padding range, names the technique ("gallery emptiness"), describes the tension between compressed text and expanded space, and states what is NOT used (no color variation) which is equally important.
440: 
441: ---
442: 
443: ### 9. Agent Prompt Guide
444: 
445: **BAD:**
446: > "Create a card component using the design system's colors, typography, and spacing. It should look like the rest of the site."
447: 
448: **GOOD:**
449: > "Design a card: white background, 1px solid #e5edf5 border, 6px radius. Shadow: rgba(50,50,93,0.25) 0px 30px 45px -30px, rgba(0,0,0,0.1) 0px 18px 36px -18px. Title at 22px sohne-var weight 300, letter-spacing -0.22px, color #061b31, 'ss01'. Body at 16px weight 300, #64748d."
450: 
451: **Why the good version works:** Every single value needed to build the card is present. The AI tool receiving this prompt has zero ambiguity about any visual property.
452: 
453: ---
454: 
455: ### 10. Section Opening
456: 
457: **BAD:**
458: > "In this section, we'll explore the depth and elevation system used throughout the design. Shadows play an important role in creating visual hierarchy."
459: 
460: **GOOD:**
461: > "Stripe's shadow system is built on a principle of chromatic depth. Where most design systems use neutral gray or black shadows, Stripe's primary shadow color (`rgba(50,50,93,0.25)`) is a deep blue-gray that echoes the brand's navy palette."
462: 
463: **Why the good version works:** No throat-clearing. Immediately states the principle (chromatic depth), names the specific technique (blue-tinted shadows), gives the exact value, and contrasts with the conventional approach.
464: 
465: ---
466: 
467: ## 12. SHADOW PHILOSOPHY PATTERN
468: 
469: Every DESIGN.md should include a shadow philosophy paragraph. This paragraph answers: "What is the THEORY behind this system's shadow usage?"
470: 
471: ### Structure
472: 
473: 1. Name the principle (chromatic depth, shadow-as-border, luminance stepping)
474: 2. Contrast with the conventional approach
475: 3. Explain the architectural benefit
476: 4. Provide 1-2 specific values as evidence
477: 
478: ### Example
479: 
480: > "Vercel has arguably the most sophisticated shadow system in modern web design. Rather than using shadows for elevation in the traditional Material Design sense, Vercel uses multi-value shadow stacks where each layer has a distinct architectural purpose: one creates the 'border' (0px spread, 1px), another adds ambient softness (2px blur), another handles depth at distance (8px blur with negative spread), and an inner ring (`#fafafa`) creates the subtle highlight that makes the card 'glow' from within."
481:

506: ## 14. FINAL QUALITY GATE
507: 
508: Before publishing a Style Reference, run these checks:
509: 
510: - [ ] Tagline passes the "could this describe three other sites?" test -- NO
511: - [ ] Zero banned words in descriptive prose
512: - [ ] Intro paragraph (4-6 sentences) has every claim mapped to a real value
513: - [ ] Colours are NAMED evocatively; every name maps to a `--color-<slug>` token; no `--_color-primitives` var leaked
514: - [ ] Components are NAMED by function (Primary CTA, Card, Badge) — no "Variant-N" or "div"
515: - [ ] Values are embedded in prose (not standalone facts) in narrative sections
516: - [ ] Values are standalone and scannable in the pre-rendered tables and component specs
517: - [ ] Every Do/Don't cites a concrete value and reads as an instruction
518: - [ ] Every agent prompt is self-contained (copy-paste ready, no doc lookups)
519: - [ ] No transition phrases ("let's look at," "in this section")
520: - [ ] No frequency dumps in prose — frequency decides prominence, it is never printed
521: - [ ] Elevation is honest: "flat" stated plainly when 0 shadows, never dressed up as "gradient-as-depth"
522: - [ ] No false SYSTEM asserted (no "focus is consistent" when the data says otherwise)
523: - [ ] Pre-rendered sections (Colors, Spacing & Shapes, Surfaces, Quick Start) pasted UNCHANGED
524: - [ ] Information density: no sentence survives the deletion test without losing information
